title: Cold retarding sourdough overnight in the fridge
subtitle: Why bakers slow-proof in the fridge and what it does for flavour, crust, and workability
excerpt: Cold retarding places the shaped sourdough loaf in the fridge for 8 to 16 hours instead of proofing at room temperature. The cold slows fermentation to a near-standstill, building complex sour flavour from the acetic acid produced at low temperature. The loaf bakes from cold, which is firmer, easier to score, and often produces better crust colour.
sourceNotes: Cold retarding as a sourdough technique is widely established in contemporary home sourdough baking. The effect of cold temperature on acetic versus lactic acid production is well-documented in practical baking literature.

recipe.yieldDescription: Technique for any shaped sourdough loaf

glossaryTerms.definition: Slowing or stopping fermentation by placing shaped dough in a refrigerator. The cold dramatically reduces yeast and bacterial activity, extending the proof window from hours to a day or more.
One of the two main organic acids produced by sourdough fermentation. Acetic acid (vinegar-type acid) is produced more at lower temperatures and gives sourdough a sharp, pronounced tang.

content.text: slows fermentation. The shaped loaf sits in the fridge overnight instead of proofing at room temperature. Three things happen: sour flavour builds from
production; the dough becomes firmer and easier to score; and baking fits into a normal day (shape before bed, bake in the morning).
Shape the loaf after bulk fermentation and place it seam-side up in a well-floured banneton or in a bowl lined with a well-floured cloth.
Cover with the cloth or a loose plastic bag and place in the fridge. Most home fridges run at 3 to 5°C. The dough will continue to ferment slowly throughout the retard.
Score and bake from cold. There is no need to bring the dough to room temperature first. A cold loaf is easier to score cleanly and often produces a more dramatic ear than a room-temperature loaf.
8 to 12 hours: standard overnight retard. Mild sour note, open crumb, clean ear.
12 to 16 hours: deeper flavour, more pronounced tang. Still gives good results with a strong starter.
Beyond 24 hours: the dough can continue to ferment slowly and will eventually overproof. Check after 20 hours; if it has risen significantly and feels very light, bake immediately.

Room-temperature proofing takes 1 to 3 hours and requires attention. Cold retarding stretches that window to most of a day and lets the baker work around a normal schedule. The flavour and crust of a retarded loaf are also noticeably better, the longer, cooler fermentation builds complexity that a quick warm proof does not.
